title: TB2-02064
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX, who alleges to be a citizen of Sri Lanka, claims to be in need of refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant is a 49-year old Tamil man from XXXX, just north of Jaffna in Northern Sri Lanka. In the 1990's his family experienced the difficulties of the civil war. He was operating a XXXX XXXX XXXX. He alleges that between 1999 and 2001, he was picked up with others and used as human shields by the Sri Lankan Army (SLA) during battles with the Liberation Tigers of Tamil Eelam (LTTE). The LTTE tried to recruit him, but he refused to join. He recounts the following bad experiences, which the panel notes occurred after the war ended in May 2009:

In XXXX, 2010, while he was away at XXXX XXXX, 3 unknown men came to his house and demanded 2 lakhs of rupees from his wife. When she said she did not have any money, they took away her jewellery and warned her not to report this.

In XXXX, 2010, 2 unknown men came to his house that night, took him in a white van blindfolded and held in a dilapidated house, where there were 5 other people. The men demanded 2 lakhs of rupees from his wife, which his father-in-law paid, and he was released after 2 days.

In XXXX 2011, on his way to the market XXXX XXXX XXXX, he was taken by 3 army and 2 paramilitary men (likely EPDP men) in a white van and detained at the XXXX army camp, where he was questioned with beating and threats about supporting the LTTE in the past, which he denied. He was released the next day after his father-in-law paid the bribe his captors demanded.

After that, his father-in-law and an agent they hired took him to Colombo, where the agent completed arrangements for his departure. In XXXX 2011, he left Sri Lanka, passed through a few countries, including about 2 months in the U. S. A., arriving in Canada on XXXX XXXX, 2012.
The panel finds that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor person in need of protection.
The panel is satisfied, on a balance of probabilities, as to the claimant's identity and that he is a citizen of Sri Lanka based on copies of his identification documents as tendered into evidence.2

The panel notes that although he had been detained and questioned by the SLA and EPDP about supporting the LTTE, he had been released, albeit after payment of a bribe. During his oral testimony, he admitted he has or had no criminal record in Sri Lanka, and never been charged criminally before a judge. He also admitted he had no problems going through checkpoints on his way to Colombo prior to his leaving the country, and that his agent did not have any problem applying for and getting his Sri Lankan passport from the government passport office. He had no problem from government security and immigration officials when exiting the country through the country's main international airport at Katunayake. He said that an airport official examined his passport against his computer and let him through. He said that a person at the gate was asking everyone for a bribe, but this was nothing specific on the claimant, who in fact did not have any money at that time to give the man, but still the man let him though.

It is known that government officials use the airport and major border points to screen and apprehend suspected LTTE members and sympathisers.3 The fact that government security or immigration officials let him go (did not apprehend him) is a strong indication to the panel that he is neither on the security watch list of the government or a wanted person. Even if his agent had bribed a security or immigration official, it is not likely the claimant would have been let through against orders on risk that the official himself could be charged with treason for aiding a suspected LTTE supporter or member.
The panel, therefore, believes, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not viewed by the government security forces as an LTTE member or supporter.

Furthermore, he admitted that during his stay in the U.S., his story was found by a U.S. asylum officer to be credible and he was referred to an immigration judge, who informed him that his claim for asylum was being considered. However, he left for Canada before that decision rendered. When the panel asked him why he left, effectively abandoning his claim, he said it was because he did not have any relatives or acquaintances in the U.S. However, the panel notes that his Personal Information Form (PIF) does not show or list any such people in Canada, as well.4

The panel, also, notes that he has not reported any problems that his wife and children, who have since been living in XXXX,5 have experienced since he left them to come to Canada. The panel draws from this a strong inference that he most likely could also be safe there with them.

The panel further notes that the claimant has not adduced any persuasive and reliable corroborating document to prove that he faces a risk of persecution or harm in returning to Sri Lanka. Although it is an established principle that oral testimony be given evidentiary weight over the lack of corroborative documentary evidence, Maldonado asserts the latter be given prominence where there are serious doubts to the claimant's story, as there are in this case.6 Furthermore, according to Rule 11, "The claimant must provide acceptable documents establishing their identity and other elements of the claim." The claimant, in this case, has not adduced such persuasive evidence.

Furthermore, the panel notes that the claimant does not fit any of the risk profiles identified in the 2012 UNHCR (United Nations High Commission on Refugees) guidelines, as particularly targeted or viewed with suspicion by the Sri Lankan government security forces.7 He was simply a XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. There is no indication in his testimony that he was an activist or a member of an activist organization. The fact that the claimant originates from an area previously controlled by the LTTE does not in itself result in a need for international refugee protection in the sense of the 1951 Convention and its 1967 Protocol. The fact he was a Tamil male from the North does not by itself indicate he faces a risk were he to return to Sri Lanka. There is insufficient credible and persuasive evidence before the panel to show the claimant fits any of the risk profiles set out in these 2012 UNHCR guidelines.

From the foregoing, the panel does not believe the claimant is wanted by or being sought by the government security forces, and, therefore, does not believe the existence of his subjective or objective basis of his fear.

As to his alleged fear of the paramilitary group EPDP, or even rogue members of the security forces, the panel adds a discussion on s. 97-Generalized Risk, as per his allegations his family or relatives had been robbed or extorted by the EPDP and forced to pay bribes for his release. Furthermore, having lived abroad in a Western country, i.e. Canada, he could be viewed as having money. Rogue members of the EPDP and security forces have taken on "criminal characteristics," engaging in robbery and extortion as they consolidate their revenue sources, taking advantage of the relatively rough conditions in the aftermath of the civil war.8 The claimant, thus, would be part of a sub-category of the general population, who would be viewed as those perceived to have money or perceived to have potential for extortion.
Following the foregoing line of reasoning, are two recent cases:

In Wilson, a case heard by Justice Simpson, A Jamaican businessman who faced extortion, and violent retaliation (he was shot) for non-compliance at the hands of the criminal gang. The court determined that the shooting and threats of violence, in this case, were "part and parcel" of the gang's criminal extortion business rather than a personal vendetta against the applicant.9

In Hernandez, heard by Justice Phelan, a Mexican who was threatened and stabbed by Los Zetas cartel members for refusing to sell drugs. The violence inflicted on the applicant was the result of his refusal to comply with the gang's demands.10

Also of interest is the recent Federal Court decision upholding the Board's decision in Paramanathan,11 a Sri Lanka case, as well. Other Sri Lanka cases with similar characteristics to the case at bar are Marthandan and Nageem.12
As such, the risk that he fears is excluded by paragraph 97(1)(b)(ii). That provision does not extend protection to those facing a risk that is faced generally by others in the country.13

As a matter of note, the Federal Court has determined that victims of crime,14 corruption,15 or vendettas16 generally fail to establish a link or nexus between their fear of persecution and one of the Convention grounds.

Based on the foregoing discussion, the fact he was released at all times after being questioned or detained, the fact he had no problem being issued a passport, the fact he was not apprehended but let through to exit the country through Colombo's international airport, and the fact he was not involved with any anti-Sri Lankan government activity or demonstration while out of the country persuades the panel that the claimant, on a balance of probabilities, does not face a risk of harm or persecution if he were to return to Sri Lanka today. The panel, also, therefore, believes that, on a balance of probabilities, the claimant is not a refugee sur place.

As to returnees to Sri Lanka, the United Kingdom's Country of Origin (COI) Report, 7 March 2012,17 states that those who could encounter difficulties on return are those identified with the following factors: * outstanding arrest warrant * criminal record * connection with LTTE * illegal departure from Sri Lanka * involvement with media or NGOs * lack of an ID card or other documentation
None of the above criteria apply to this claimant.

On June 17, 2011, the United Kingdom Board Agency (UKBA) returned 26 asylum seekers from Sri Lanka, 15 of who were Tamil, 7 of whom were Muslims, and 4 of whom were Sinhalese. When the returnees arrived at Colombo, they were all questioned by the CID. After questioning, no arrests or criminal charges were laid against the rejected asylum seekers and they were all returned to their homes.18

Documentary sources state that returning Tamils are subjected to the same screening process as for all persons returning to Sri Lanka, regardless of whether they are returning on a voluntary basis or as the result of a failed refugee claim, and that "the process is not impacted by ethnicity." The authorities are mainly "seeking information about human trafficking and smuggling from the country."19 Once a returnee's right to enter the country has been established, they are then interviewed at the airport by the CID (Criminal Investigation Division), followed by an interview by the State Intelligence Service (SIS). The CID conducts criminal background checks of returnees by contacting the police stations in all the districts in which the returnee lived. Generally, these police record checks may be completed in a few hours, but can last 24 to 48 hours.20 However, in circumstances where it is difficult to obtain security clearance, these detentions may at times last for periods of up to some months.21

The Canadian High Commission has noted that there have only been 4 cases of persons having been detained upon arrival of which the Canada High Commission is aware of, and these cases involved outstanding criminal charges in-country and were not related to their overseas asylum claims or their ethnicity.22
The recently issued 2012 UNHCR Guidelines did not indicate any noteworthy change in the information regarding the plight of returnees to Sri Lanka.

The Federal Court has held that pursuant to IRPA section 97(1): (i) there must be persuasive evidence (i.e. on a balance of probabilities) establishing the facts on which a claimant relies to say that he or she faces a substantial danger of being tortured or of having cruel and unusual treatment or punishment inflicted upon his or her return; and (ii) the danger or risk must be such that it is more likely than not that he or she would be tortured or subjected to other cruel and degrading treatments.23
In the case of this particular claimant, the panel finds, based on the foregoing analysis, that there is no such persuasive evidence he faces those risks or would likely suffer those treatments.
The panel, also, is of the view that, based on the evidence adduced, there is no concern for compelling reasons in this case. Summation
The panel has taken into account the oral submissions by Counsel.

Having considered all of the evidence adduced, the panel determines that there is not a seriously possibility that the claimant would be persecuted in Sri Lanka or that, on a balance of probabilities, he would be personally subjected to a danger of torture or face a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment if he were to return to Sri Lanka today.

The Refugee Protection Division, therefore, determines that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee within the meaning of section 96 of the IRPA nor person in need of protection under subsection 97(1). His claim is, therefore, rejected. (signed) "W. Lim" W.
